items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: One time you mentioned something to me... what about the man in your band that did that? >> [INTERVIEWEE] Well, that was Geechee Robinson.

ctx.x: Okay, and we're at 910 Royal Street, so we're going to just proceed on. One time you mentioned something to me, and I don't want to mention it by the day, but I thought it was a very interesting point, something that the psychologists talk about. That is, how the guys, some people will change, like they're, with the moon, as the moon changes. Right. And they, what about the man in your band that did that?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-12-30
items.q: when we added Geechee Robinson, another drum roll. ... I had Nick Turner on the Suze for MWM on the drum roll.

ctx.x: So you got a real close song, didn't you?

That was the first bass song. And then when we went up a little further, when we added Geechee Robinson, another drum roll. We had Nick Turner, another bass record. I had Jimmy Johnson on the string bass. And I had Nick Turner on the Suze for MWM on the drum roll. And then later on I added Harold Holmes, who's now in Canada, who did most of my arranging. And as we traveled over the country, I added here, subtracted, added and subtracted.
And I found the change in the years. Did you ever play any other state fairs? You want to start it by now or is it?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: After he left my band. Yeah.

ctx.x: Well, you had Frank Jackay. Strictly a section man. Yeah. Geechee Robinson. Where did Frank Jackay come from? Lake Charles, Louisiana. Cousin to Illinois.
Who did he play with, Frank?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1974-01-01
items.q: And then too we had the language of our own... we always suspected Geechee Robinson. But we never was able to pin it on him... Geechee, I told you, he was right.

ctx.x: Your wife reminded us about Ben having her own language and chick keys and doing a restaurant.

Yeah, different things like that. And for instance, we would come to town and the menu had certain prices when it came for us to pay. It was a nickel, a dime, a quarter moment was on the menu. So you would ask the guy about that and you would tell you, well that's the end for the people in town. Out of town people had a different price. And then too we had the language of our own. We had the chick keys meant to stop talking, somebody was listening. Then we had the, what you call the hawk in the band. And then we…
